structure.title: 3. The Confederate diaspora: push and pull factors
4. Transmitting and entrenching Confederate culture (measures, identification, results)
7. A legacy of inequity and exclusion
Acknowledgments, Supplementary Data, Data Availability, References

observations.statement: The core design is named a shift-share instrumental variable (SSIV) framework: 1870 cross-county migrant network shares combined with predicted 1870 to 1900 origin-state migration shifts, with the estimand described as the distinct influence of the postbellum diaspora conditional on the 1870 Southern-born share.

Two interrelated threats are stated before the estimator: place-specific confounders such as factor endowments, and endogenous location choice; the authors argue the sign of OLS bias is ambiguous depending on economic versus ideological sorting.

The exclusion argument follows the push-factor SSIV logic: shares may be endogenous, so identification rests on shifts predicted from origin-county push factors, citing Borusyak, Hull and Jaravel; relevance is argued from chain migration along antebellum pathways.
observations.quote: can satisfy the exclusion restriction even when the share component is endogenous

observations.statement: The IV estimate is explicitly interpreted as a LATE for counties with the strongest chain migration; the authors report the share of positive Rotemberg weights and name the origin state driving negative weights, following Goldsmith-Pinkham, Sorkin and Swift.
Controlling for the 1870 Southern White share is presented as making the IV specification equivalent to one in changes, absorbing time-invariant heterogeneity in initial shares.

Predicted shifts are built by LASSO on origin-county push factors plus their squares and interactions, applied to two census periods and aggregated to sending states; the paper writes out the prediction and aggregation equations.

The 1870 base year is chosen over 1860 because many Western counties were not yet incorporated; the share of counties lacking data in each base year is reported and an 1860 base year is used as a robustness check.

Four binary county outcomes (memorials, UDC chapters, second KKK chapters, lynchings of Black people) are summed into a composite index; each source, the time window, and the post-1900 restriction are spelled out in text and figure notes.
The treatment regressor is the 1900 county share of White residents born in the eleven former Confederate states plus Oklahoma; the inclusion of Oklahoma is justified in a footnote.
observations.locator: Section 3, footnote 6; Section 3 Destination pull factors

observations.statement: Confederate place names are matched conservatively using a restrictive set of distinguishing names to minimise false positives; a footnote reports that stricter name-length rules give similar estimates and refers to appendix tables by memorial type.
Baseline controls are log 1870 population and log county area; all continuous controls enter quadratically, with additional interactive nonlinearities in robustness.

Individuals are tracked with complete-count censuses 1870 to 1900 and Census Tree linked records; the paper describes the linking sources and notes in a footnote that the 1890 microdata were lost in a fire.

Slaveholders are linked from the 1860 Slave Schedule to the population census by name and county using the ABE algorithm with NYSIIS-standardised names; the match rate is reported and benchmarked against linking rates in cited studies.

The county sample excludes former Confederate states and Oklahoma; observation counts are reported in every table and the paper states in text when subsamples shrink (border-state exclusion, Western counties, authority-worker cutoff).

The occupational-authority interaction analysis restricts to counties with more than a minimum number of authority workers; the footnote gives the resulting sample size and cites an appendix table for alternative cutoffs.

KKK membership rosters for Denver, Indiana and Arizona are matched to White men in the 1920 census using ABE with NYSIIS names; the footnote reports match rates before and after accounting for non-unique names and refers to reweighting checks.

The main table stacks OLS in panel (a) and SSIV in panel (b) for the same five outcomes, alternates columns without and with sorting controls, lists FE and control blocks as Yes rows, and reports adjusted R2 (OLS), observations, and outcome means.
Every table note ends with the clustering statement (60 by 60 mile grid cells following Bester, Conley and Hansen) and the three-level star convention.
No regression weights are mentioned for any county-level or individual-level specification; equations and table notes describe unweighted regressions.

Clustering by square grid cells is justified by citing Bester et al., and robustness to other spatial structures (Conley HAC, Adao et al. shift-share SEs) is announced in the design section and delegated to the appendix.
observations.locator: Section 4.2; Section 4.3 Identification and robustness checks

observations.statement: Individual-level regressions cluster at the level of the fixed effect: origin county by year for selection, destination county for occupational sorting, destination county by year for the linked slaveholder sample, and enumeration district for KKK membership. No further justification is given.
observations.locator: Table 1 notes; Section 5.2; Figure 5 notes; Table 7 notes

observations.statement: IV tables report a first-stage F-statistic, Anderson-Rubin p-value, Kleibergen-Paap underidentification p-value, and a Hausman exogeneity p-value as rows, with each null hypothesis explained in the table notes.
The first-stage estimates for the main table are relegated to an appendix table and described in the text as strong.
observations.locator: Section 4.3, first paragraph; Appendix Table B.1

observations.statement: With multiple endogenous regressors, tables report Sanderson-Windmeijer conditional F-statistics and underidentification p-values per endogenous variable alongside the joint KP statistic; a footnote acknowledges that joint strength can be weaker than individual strength.

A placebo-type outcome check compares effects on lynchings of Black people with lynchings of non-Black minorities and Whites, reported in an appendix table, to separate racially targeted violence from generalised honour-culture violence.
The Adao, Kolesar and Morales random-shifts placebo exercise is implemented to validate the shift-based identifying variation; it is mentioned in the design section and reported in the appendix.

Placebo occupations with similar size and occupational score but no public-facing authority are constructed for the institutional-leverage interaction; the table notes list the placebo occupations for each category.
For the slaveholder versus non-slaveholder SSIVs the paper reports the correlation between the two instruments and explains that predicting 1870 shares with a gravity model was needed to reduce it.

Robustness is summarised in one short paragraph listing four families (alternative SEs, control sets, sorting specifications, alternative origin and destination definitions) and pointing to an appendix section rather than a main-text table.
observations.locator: Section 4.3, Identification and robustness checks; Appendix B.3

observations.statement: Sending and receiving states are dropped one at a time, summarised as an appendix figure, motivated by the negative Rotemberg weights of one origin state.

Coefficient stability when adding all heterogeneity moderators as controls is reported in a footnote citing an appendix table, and is used to argue the heterogeneity results are not an artefact of residual sorting.

KKK membership results are shown in the main table with no FE, county FE and enumeration-district FE side by side, and the text lists appendix robustness to non-unique matches, U.S.-born restriction, and occupation FE.

Heterogeneity is framed by the conceptual framework: origin-side ideological intensity and destination-side malleability are each tested by interacting the treatment with standardised moderators, instrumented by SSIV times moderator, with the own term in both stages.

Separate SSIVs are built for migrant subgroups (border, upper South, deep South; Union North by slavery history) and the sample is restricted to the relevant destination region for each comparison, as stated in the table notes.
Origin-state moderators are aggregated to the destination county as migrant-weighted averages; the weighting formula is written explicitly in the text.

Channels are tested with micro-data: occupational choice regressions with county FE for authority positions, and KKK membership regressions for first- and second-generation migrants and for non-Southern neighbours identified from consecutive census entries.
observations.locator: Sections 5.2 and 6.1; Figures 4 to 6; Tables 7 and 8

observations.statement: Neighbour spill-over estimates are labelled suggestive; the authors explicitly list alternative explanations (correlated joining, reverse transmission) and argue against one using the earlier table.
observations.quote: they are not dispositive of one-way transmission

observations.statement: The institutional-leverage interaction is described as suggestive but not conclusive, distinguishing the causally interpreted overall diaspora effect from the occupational representation term that may be confounded by destination choice.

Effects are interpreted per percentage point of migrant share relative to the outcome mean, and as the move from zero to the mean diaspora share; the mean and standard deviation of the regressor are given in text so readers can scale.

A more-than-compositional argument compares the IV coefficient with what a purely mechanical composition effect would imply, and a footnote gives a back-of-envelope share of KKK membership attributable to the diaspora under a causal assumption.

The OLS versus IV gap is discussed at length, attributing it to measurement error in historical data, economic versus ideological sorting, and a LATE among aggrieved compliers; for the slaveholder analysis the gap is partly attributed to linkage measurement error with an appendix exercise.
Interaction effects are interpreted at one standard deviation of the moderator, with the moderator mean and SD reported in a footnote to translate the standardised term.

Authors state that county-level models cannot separate the relative roles of spill-overs, organisations and institutions, and that linked slaveholder samples carry more measurement error than the complete-count baseline regressor.
For the sundown-town outcome the authors note that some Black depopulation may have been voluntary rather than forced.
The KKK micro analysis centres on Denver because comprehensive data exist, and is extended to Indiana and Arizona explicitly to generalise beyond a setting where supremacist targeting differed.

The authors contrast the 1870 to 1900 wave with the later 20th-century Southern White migration, showing in appendix figures that occupational sorting and selection patterns reverse over time, and frame the framework as applicable to other migrations.

Figures are county maps of the regressor and composite outcome, a moving-average time series of naming frequencies by group, and coefficient plots with confidence intervals normalised by comparison-group means; summary statistics and full estimates behind figures are in appendix tables.
observations.locator: Figures 1 to 6; Appendix Tables A.1, C.3 to C.5

observations.statement: Table notes restate the sample, the instrument construction, control groups by reference to the main table's notes, data sources for moderators, and the null of each diagnostic; appendix tables and figures are lettered by appendix section (A, B, C, D).
The selection table reports a non-migrant mean row and marks the controls row with a dash when absent, distinguishing demographic and labour-market panels.
The introduction previews every empirical section with specific findings, then gives four contribution paragraphs positioned against distinct literatures and a roadmap paragraph naming each section.

Order is conceptual framework, historical background, descriptive selection and sorting, outcome measurement, identification, baseline results, then heterogeneity (conditions) and mechanisms (channels), then consequences; robustness is not a separate section and most checks live in the online appendix.
A conceptual framework with two conditions and three channels is introduced first and each later section opens by stating which element of the framework it tests.
A Data Availability statement cites a Zenodo replication package DOI providing code and publicly available data, and states that it documents the data that are not publicly available.
All appendices are referenced as Supplementary Material available online; none are included in the PDF, and no software is named in the main text.

Data combine public complete-count censuses and Census Tree links, public digital collections (SPLC, GNIS, TIGER, NCES, VCU Klan map, lynching datasets), newly digitised UDC minutes, and KKK ledgers obtained from an archive, other researchers, and a family archivist by direct outreach.

The descriptive push and pull regressions in Section 3 are explicitly framed as setting the stage for the instrument: the push-factor regression later becomes the LASSO shift predictor and the pull factors become the sorting controls.

gaps: No explicit justification for the grid-cell cluster size beyond citing Bester, Conley and Hansen.
No multiple-testing adjustment across the five outcomes or the many heterogeneity moderators.
No software or package named in the main text.
No balance table for the instrument; instrument validity is supported by the random-shifts placebo and control-set checks in the appendix.
No preregistration or ethics statement (historical public and archival data).
Appendix contents (Supplementary Material) are not in the PDF, so appendix practices are recorded only as referenced from the main text.

reading.note: All 48 PDF pages read, including tables, footnotes, acknowledgments, data availability and references. The paper has no in-PDF appendix; Appendices A to D are online Supplementary Material and were not available, so appendix observations rely on main-text references.
